title: Qwen3.8 Flash-Next W4A16 Agentic LoRA Delta
subtitle: LoRA fine-tune of Intel W4A16 Qwen3.8-Flash-Next; delta shards, needs the base
description:
# Model Summary

A merged LoRA fine-tune of **Qwen3.8-Flash-Next** in Intel's **W4A16 AutoRound** quantization, trained for multi-turn agentic tool use. The data is the base model's own successful episodes: it solved grid-based puzzle environments by writing and running Python in a REPL tool.

This instance is a **delta overlay**, not a standalone checkpoint. It holds only the 14 safetensors shards whose tensors the fine-tune changed (≈72.3 GB) plus configuration files. Every other file comes unchanged from the base instance [`dfranzen/intel-qwen3.8-flash-next-w4a16-autoround`](https://www.kaggle.com/models/dfranzen/intel-qwen3.8-flash-next-w4a16-autoround) (Transformers / default / 1). See *Usage*.

**Result in one line:** the fine-tune lowered held-out next-reply loss (0.859 → 0.650), but it **scored below the base model** in our downstream agent evaluations (see *Evaluation Results*). We publish it as a research artifact, not as an improvement over the base model.

## Credits: what is not ours

- **Base model:** [Qwen3.8-Flash-Next](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next) by the Qwen team, under the Qwen Community License 1.0.
- **Quantization:** [Intel/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-W4A16-AutoRound](https://huggingface.co/Intel/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-W4A16-AutoRound) by Intel, made with [AutoRound](https://github.com/intel/auto-round) (arXiv:2309.05516).
- **Kaggle reshard of that checkpoint:** [dfranzen/intel-qwen3.8-flash-next-w4a16-autoround](https://www.kaggle.com/models/dfranzen/intel-qwen3.8-flash-next-w4a16-autoround) by Daniel Franzen. Its weights are unchanged, only redistributed across files. This instance's shard layout follows it.
- **Puzzle environments used to generate the training episodes:** an open-source, MIT-licensed collection of about 250 community-made grid-puzzle games. They are not ours.

**Our contribution:** generating and filtering the training episodes, the LoRA training, merging the LoRA into the BF16 tensors, and the evaluations reported here.

# Usage

The instance overrides 14 of the base checkpoint's 17 main shards. `MANIFEST.json` lists the replaced files under `replaced_shards`. Build one model directory: link every file of the base instance into it, then point the listed shards to this instance.

```python
import json, os, kagglehub

base = kagglehub.model_download("dfranzen/intel-qwen3.8-flash-next-w4a16-autoround/transformers/default/1")
delta = kagglehub.model_download("ravinderonkaggle/flashnext-arc3-recipe-v3/transformers/default/1")
replaced = {s["file"] for s in json.load(open(os.path.join(delta, "MANIFEST.json")))["replaced_shards"]}

out = "/kaggle/working/qwen38-flash-next-ft"
os.makedirs(out, exist_ok=True)
for name in os.listdir(base):
    src = os.path.join(delta if name in replaced else base, name)
    os.symlink(src, os.path.join(out, name))
# `out` now loads exactly like the base checkpoint (same config, tokenizer and chat template).
```

On Kaggle, attach both models as notebook inputs and use their `/kaggle/input/...` paths instead of `kagglehub`.

Serve or load `out` with any runtime that supports the base checkpoint, for example a recent vLLM or SGLang with AutoRound/W4A16 support. We ran it with both. Use the same chat template, reasoning settings and sampling parameters as for the base model.

# System

- **Model type:** a decoder-only language model with mixture-of-experts layers and a vision encoder, inherited from the base model.
- **Input:** text and images. Our training used multi-turn chats with a system prompt, user turns that include rendered images of the environment state, assistant turns with reasoning and tool calls, and tool results.
- **Output:** text, including reasoning and tool calls.
- **Upstream dependency:** the base instance's unchanged files are required. These are 3 main shards (00002, 00016, 00017), the n-gram (PLE) table shards, `model_extra_tensors.safetensors` and the other base files. This instance is not usable on its own.

# Implementation requirements

- **Training hardware:** a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU (96 GB; a Google Colab G4 runtime) with about 177 GB of host RAM.
- **How the base model was trained:**
  - the int4 routed experts stayed frozen and were dequantized per routed expert;
  - the BF16 n-gram (PLE) table was memory-mapped from host memory;
  - LoRA adapters were attached to BF16 linear layers only.
- **Speed:** about 36–41 s per optimizer step (4 windows of up to 10,240 tokens), roughly 800–870 tokens per second.
- **Training time:** stage 1 took about 12 hours (resumed once after a runtime restart); stage 2 took about 4 hours.
- **Inference:** the same as the base model.

# Model Characteristics

## Model initialization

Fine-tuned from the base checkpoint described above. Stage 2 continued from the stage 1 adapter with a fresh optimizer and schedule.

## Model stats

| | |
|---|---|
| LoRA | rank 16, alpha 32 |
| Layers with LoRA | BF16 linear layers: attention q/k/v/o; linear-attention `in_proj_qkv`, `in_proj_z`, `out_proj`; shared expert `gate`/`up`/`down` |
| Tensors changed | 300 (merged in FP32, stored in BF16) |
| Unchanged | int4 routed experts, n-gram (PLE) table, MTP layer, vision encoder, embeddings |
| Files in this instance | 14 main shards (≈72.3 GB) + `MANIFEST.json` + configuration and tokenizer files |

## Other details

The LoRA is merged into the weights; no adapter files are included. No pruning or further quantization was applied: the changed tensors are BF16, as in the base checkpoint.

# Data Overview

## Training data

Self-generated, verified agent episodes (rejection-sampling fine-tuning):

1. The base model played about 250 grid-puzzle environments through a Python REPL tool and an image view of the environment.
2. From each episode we kept only the assistant turns that worked on a task the environment confirmed as completed. Every other turn stayed only as context.
3. Episodes were packed into multi-turn sequences, then cut into training windows of up to 10,240 tokens. Loss was computed on the kept assistant turns only.

| | Stage 1 | Stage 2 |
|---|---|---|
| Source episodes | first self-play round over 249 environments | second self-play round over 75 harder environments |
| Environments with kept data | 214 | 44 |
| Completed tasks kept | 1,010 | 121 (41 of them not solved in round 1) |
| Sequences / supervised assistant turns | 463 / 9,857 | 100 / 1,957 (99 sequences after removing the held-out environments) |
| Tokens | ≈27.9M in sequences, ≈8.1M supervised | — |
| Training windows | 4,730 | 1,041 new + 520 replayed from stage 1 |
| Schedule | 1 epoch, 1,183 steps, LR 1e-4 cosine | 1 epoch, 391 steps, LR 5e-5 cosine |

No outputs of other language models were used. All supervised text was written by the base model itself.

## Evaluation data

- **Held-out loss:** 6 environments were excluded from training: 24 windows, 38,043 target tokens.
- **Agent evaluation:** a separate set of 25 interactive puzzle environments, none of them used in training.

# Evaluation Results

## Summary

**Held-out next-reply cross-entropy**, measured on the 6 held-out environments:

| Checkpoint | Loss |
|---|---|
| Base | 0.859 |
| After stage 1 | 0.6485 |
| After stage 2 (this model) | 0.6502 |

**Downstream agent score** on the 25 held-out environments. The score runs from 0 to 100 and rewards completing tasks with few actions. Each figure is a single run.

| Setup | Base model | Stage 1 | **This model** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Agent harness A, 2.5 h | 52.98 (114 tasks) | 39.03 (95) | **43.43 (101)** |
| Agent harness B, 9,000 s | 47.12 (101) | — | **36.73 (96)** |

The paired per-environment difference, this model minus base, was −9.55 points (SE 5.77) in harness A and −10.39 points (SE 5.50) in harness B.

In harness A the two arms differed only in the weights. In harness B, this model's run also used newer inference-engine and harness components than the base model's run, so that comparison is not a clean weights-only pair.

In harness B, at equal playing time, this model took **8,659 actions against about 5,300** for the base model. The completed tasks were similar (96 vs 101), so the lower score comes mainly from using more actions per task.

## Subgroup evaluation results

None.

# Fairness

The training data consists of synthetic puzzle environments and the base model's own outputs. It contains no data about people or demographic groups. Fairness properties are inherited from the base model and were not evaluated.

# Usage limitations

- It does **not** outperform the base model on our downstream evaluations. Prefer the base model unless you are studying this kind of fine-tune.
- What we think caused the regression, for anyone repeating this recipe:
  - **Turns without a tool call:** 3.05% of supervised turns contain no tool call.
  - **Inefficient episodes were kept:** on first attempts at a new environment, the kept solutions used a median 1.8× and a 90th percentile 18× the actions of the shortest solution. The model learned to act more.
  - **Suggested fix:** filter for efficient episodes and drop turns without a tool call before training.
- It is narrowly trained on one tool format and one domain, so behavior elsewhere may differ from the base model in ways we did not measure.
- It needs the base instance's files. See *Usage*.

# Ethics

- The model writes and runs code through a tool. Run generated code only in a sandbox.
- No additional safety tuning or red-teaming was done beyond the base model's.
